name: AI News
blurb: Daily AI news from the publishers who broke it, split into headline coverage of the field and vendor announcements from the companies building it. Every story links to the original source, and any claim quoted in our coverage is cross-referenced against the laws, lawsuits, companies, tools, papers, and people already tracked in this atlas.

domains.name: AI Headline News
domains.blurb: The day's most consequential AI stories across law, policy, research, safety, and society, curated from 34 vetted feeds. Each item carries the original publisher link and a note on how it connects to the bills, cases, and frameworks tracked elsewhere on this site.

domains.name: AI Vendor News
domains.blurb: Product launches, model releases, pricing changes, and company announcements from the AI vendors themselves. Each item links to the vendor's original announcement and cross-references the company's profile in our AI Companies directory where one exists.

domains.name: This Week in AI
domains.blurb: A weekly record of what moved in AI policy and litigation, permalinked by ISO week.

domains.name: AI Historical Timeline
domains.blurb: From the 1940s to the present: Turing, the perceptron, expert systems, backpropagation, deep learning, AlexNet, transformers, and what followed.

reading.body:
The site tracks 452 pages of AI news across four sections, with 436 pages devoted to daily headline coverage from 34 vetted feeds and 15 pages of weekly policy and litigation summaries, but vendor announcements comprise only 1 page.

The disparity reflects what reaches public attention. Headline news dominates because policy, regulation, safety research, and legal action shape the operating environment for AI systems. These stories determine what compute can be built, where buildings can be sited, and how power infrastructure gets allocated. Vendor announcements, by contrast, are promotional and often ephemeral. They document product launches and pricing changes, not the structural constraints that matter for scaling.

The coverage links each story to original sources and cross-references claims against tracked laws, lawsuits, companies, and people elsewhere on the atlas. This architecture assumes that AI news cannot be evaluated in isolation. A company announcement about a new model only makes sense against the regulatory framework it operates within, the litigation it may trigger, and the infrastructure decisions it implies.

What this data does not show is which stories drive outcomes. A single policy change might constrain the entire industry. A thousand vendor announcements might pass unnoticed. The volume of headline coverage reflects only that policy, law, and safety capture more attention than vendor news, not that they matter more or less for AI's physical trajectory.
